title: Palaeoart & Speculation
keyIdea: Palaeoart is the science of drawing and modelling dinosaurs. It starts from fossils: bones, teeth, claws and footprints are real evidence. Skin colour, fat, muscles and sounds usually do not fossilise, so artists make informed guesses using living relatives such as birds and crocodiles. Rare finds fill some gaps: skin impressions show scales, quill knobs show feathers, and melanosomes can show real colour. When new fossils turn up, the pictures change, which is why Velociraptor went from scaly to feathered.
familyTip: Look at a dinosaur in a book, a toy or a film together. Point to each part and ask: would a fossil show this, or did someone choose it? Bones and teeth are evidence; colour and noises are nearly always guesses. Then look up a picture of Velociraptor from an old book and a new one, and spot what changed.

visual.caption: Evidence or guess? Drag each part of a dinosaur picture, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort fossil evidence from guesses, build a dinosaur in layers, drag through four discoveries, match rare clues and check a museum label.

kid: Nobody has ever seen a living dinosaur. So how do we have pictures of them? Scientists and artists work together. Their pictures are called palaeoart. Every good picture starts with fossils.

Hard parts last. Bones, teeth and claws can turn to stone, so we can measure them. Footprints can last too. Soft parts nearly always rot away first. That means skin, fat, muscle, eyes and colour are usually missing. Sounds leave nothing behind at all.

So artists build a dinosaur in layers. First the bones. Then muscles, using marks on the bones and animals alive today, like birds and crocodiles. Then skin or feathers. Colour comes last, and it is usually a guess. A careful guess is called speculation. It must fit the evidence, but it could be wrong.

Sometimes a rare fossil fills a gap. Skin pressed into mud can show scales. Bumps on an arm bone, called quill knobs, show where big feathers were fixed. In 2007 these were found on Velociraptor, so the old scaly pictures had to change. Tiny colour sacs in fossil feathers even showed that Sinosauropteryx had a striped ginger and white tail.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. In England this supports Year 6 science on evolution and inheritance. Pupils learn that fossils give us facts about living things from millions of years ago. It also fits working scientifically: finding evidence that supports or refutes an idea, and seeing how ideas change when new evidence turns up.

Useful terms. Palaeoart rebuilds extinct animals from fossils. Artists start with the skeleton. They add muscles using muscle scars and living relatives, birds and crocodiles. Then comes the body covering: scales, fuzz or feathers. Colour comes last. Rare fossils give direct evidence. Some Edmontosaurus fossils keep skin prints. A Velociraptor arm bone has quill knobs (Turner and others, 2007). Melanosomes showed the striped tail of Sinosauropteryx (Zhang and others, 2010).

Common mistakes to watch for. Many children think a museum model is a fact, like a photo. Others think it is all made up. Some think the dinosaurs changed when the pictures changed. A common slip is to trust films: film raptors are far bigger than the real, turkey-sized Velociraptor. Ask: which part could a fossil show, and which part did someone choose?

practice.prompt: Which part of a dinosaur is most often an artist's guess?
choices: The length of its leg bones
practice.hint: Which parts are hard enough to turn into stone?
practice.explain: Teeth and bones fossilise, so they can be measured. Colour almost never survives, so artists choose it.

practice.prompt: A dig finds {b} bones and {t} teeth from one dinosaur, but no skin. How many of these finds show its colour?
practice.hint: Do bones or teeth keep the colour of the skin?
practice.explain: 0. None of the {b} bones or {t} teeth shows skin colour, so that part of the picture is still a guess.

practice.prompt: A fossil skeleton is {=2*h} metres long, nose to tail. Half of the length is tail. How many metres long is the tail?
practice.hint: Half of a length means divide it by 2.
practice.explain: {=2*h} ÷ 2 = {h} metres of tail. Measuring bones like this is real evidence, not a guess.

practice.prompt: How do scientists know Velociraptor had feathers, when no feathers were found with it?
choices: Quill knobs on its arm bone
practice.hint: Birds have small bumps on a bone where big feathers attach.
practice.explain: In 2007 scientists found quill knobs on a Velociraptor arm bone. They only form where large feathers are fixed.

practice.prompt: Why do pictures of the same dinosaur change over the years?
choices: The dinosaur changed how it looked
practice.hint: Did the dinosaur change, or what we know about it?
practice.explain: The dinosaur was the same all along. New finds, like quill knobs and feathered fossils, changed what we know.

pool.prompt: An artist is starting a new dinosaur picture. What should they draw first?
pool.explain: The skeleton comes from real fossils. Muscles, skin and colour are added on top, each a bit less certain.

pool.prompt: Which fossil could show the pattern of a dinosaur's scales?
pool.hint: Which find is a print of the outside of the body?
pool.explain: Skin pressed into mud before it hardened can keep the shape of scales, even when the skin is gone.

pool.hint: They are tiny sacs that hold colour in feathers and skin.
pool.explain: Their shapes match colours in living birds, so in rare fossils they reveal colour, like Sinosauropteryx's striped tail.

pool.prompt: A book with a scaly Velociraptor was printed in {y}. Quill knobs were found in 2007. How many years before the find was the book printed?
pool.hint: Take the earlier year away from 2007.
pool.explain: 2007 − {y} = {=2007-y} years. Before 2007 nobody had the evidence, so the scaly picture was a fair guess for its time.

pool.prompt: A film shows Velociraptor taller than a grown-up. What do the fossils say?
choices: It was about the size of a turkey
pool.hint: We have its bones, so we can measure it.
pool.explain: The skeleton shows a turkey-sized animal, up to about 2 m long with its tail. The film made it much bigger.

choices: No: it starts from fossils and fills gaps with careful guesses
pool.hint: Think about which layers come from fossils and which do not.
pool.explain: Bones and teeth are evidence. Colour and soft parts are informed guesses that must fit the evidence.

pool.prompt: A model dinosaur has {e} parts built from fossil evidence and {g} parts that are guesses. How many parts are guesses?
pool.hint: Only count the parts that no fossil showed.
pool.explain: {g} parts are guesses. A good museum label says which ones, so visitors know.

pool.prompt: How do artists decide how big a dinosaur's muscles were?
choices: From marks on the bones and from living animals
pool.hint: Muscles leave rough scars where they join bone.
pool.explain: Muscle scars on bones, plus birds and crocodiles alive today, guide the muscle layer.
